episode.broadcastScript:
This is The Innovation Pulse for the week ending Friday, July thirty-first, twenty twenty-six. And here's who is innovating in higher education this week.

<break time="1.0s"/>

The top story this week comes from Axios, which reported ahead of Wednesday's announcement that OpenAI will give one hundred thousand academic researchers free access to its most advanced A.I. models through 2027. Selected researchers will receive access to GPT-5.6 Sol Pro, equivalent to a two-hundred-dollar-per-month subscription, at no cost. Each participant can also invite four collaborators from their academic institution.

The program targets researchers in biology, chemistry, computer science, engineering, mathematics and physics. The first ten thousand researchers will begin receiving access this summer, at institutions including the Institute for Advanced Study. OpenAI says participant data will not be used to train models, and researchers will receive business-grade privacy and security protections.

The initiative is part of a broader commitment to invest more than two hundred fifty million dollars through 2027 in external scientific research. In a statement, OpenAI said, "Our strategy is not to decide which scientific problems deserve attention or try to solve them all ourselves. It is to put capable tools in the hands of the research community and let researchers pursue the questions they know best."

The program does come with a gap, however. Researchers in A.I. fields have argued that meaningful independent evaluation requires access to model weights and training data. OpenAI says restricting that access helps prevent misuse, but researchers counter that limited access hampers independent evaluations of model behavior, reproducibility and safety. The program is aimed broadly at math and science fields, meaning the researchers most focused on auditing the technology itself are excluded from its benefits.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In Insights and Trends, Inside Higher Ed reports on a professor who has made a striking reversal. Two years ago, Scott Latham of the University of Massachusetts Lowell was among academia's most prominent critics of A.I. in higher education. In a June 2024 editorial, he urged faculty to, quote, pump the brakes on artificial intelligence, warning that robots would take their jobs.

Today, Latham not only uses A.I. in his own classroom. He has launched the A.I. Campus Index, an independent national ranking system measuring how well colleges and universities deploy A.I. for students, faculty and operations. The index scores institutions across six areas: classroom use, campus life, operations, governance, research and workforce readiness. The total possible score is 350 points, with classroom use weighted most heavily at 85 points.

Latham told Inside Higher Ed that two things shifted his view: A.I. capabilities evolved faster than he anticipated, and concerns about higher education's long-term viability deepened. He still believes A.I. will displace some faculty, specifically those who refuse to engage with it. "The faculty that it's going to put out of a job," he said, "are those that continue to resist and don't experiment."

<break time="1.0s"/>

In Case Study, when Miami Dade College launched its associate degree in applied A.I. in fall 2023, more than 750 students enrolled in A.I. courses in the first academic year alone. By fall 2025, more than 2,000 students were taking A.I. courses at the college, according to a first-person account in Issues in Science and Technology by Antonio Delgado Fornaguera, MDC's vice president of innovation and technology partnerships.

The student demographics stood out. Over the first three academic years, roughly 60% of students were older than 26, and about 30% were older than 41, experienced professionals and career changers seeking an on-ramp into applied A.I. roles.

The curriculum was built around employer input from a Business and Industry Leadership Team of A.I. professionals and hiring managers. Noelle Russell, CEO of the A.I. Leadership Institute and a BILT member, told MDC curriculum designers: "We don't need every hire to build new models from scratch. We need people who can work with data, test outputs, document decisions, and apply AI in a real process where mistakes have consequences."

MDC has since co-founded the National Applied A.I. Consortium, which has trained more than 3,000 faculty and staff across 550 colleges and universities in 48 states.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In A.I. Workforce and Careers, The New York Times reports on a pay premium reshaping the skilled trades market. Installation and maintenance jobs at data centers pay 42% more than comparable positions in other fields, according to an Indeed analysis cited by the Times, fueling intense competition for electricians, carpenters and other trades workers.

Data centers could triple their power use in the United States over the next three years, reaching 12% of the country's total electricity consumption, according to a Department of Energy-backed study.

In markets including Dallas and Northern Virginia, workers are switching employers for signing bonuses and higher per diem rates, and competition for labor is beginning to affect other sectors. Economist Mario Iacobacci told the Times: "The resources are very limited, so decisions to build one thing kind of drag from another."

Google has announced funding to train tens of thousands of new U.S. electricians, including a ten-million-dollar grant for electrical worker nonprofits. BlackRock is investing one hundred million dollars in skilled trades training. Longer-term, Jeff Strohl of Georgetown University's Center on Education and the Workforce told the Times that a smooth worker transition after data center construction peaks is, in his words, "probably not likely."

<break time="1.0s"/>

Also in A.I. Workforce and Careers, Compass Datacenters and Meridian Community College have launched Mississippi's first Mechanical, Electrical and Information Technology Data Center Pathway Program, according to The AI Journal. The 14-week program requires no degree or prior experience, and Compass is funding full-tuition scholarships for the inaugural cohort.

Ten industry partners, including Schneider Electric, Siemens, Vertiv and Rosendin, are supporting the first class, which begins this fall. The program is modeled on a Compass initiative launched in Red Oak, Texas, now in its second year. That Texas program is waitlisted, and graduates have landed positions paying 30 to 50% above local median salaries.

Meridian Community College serves more than 3,500 students annually. The data center industry, according to Compass, faces a shortfall of more than 500,000 skilled trade professionals annually.

<break time="1.0s"/>

From the Insights and Trends front, NPR reports that ninety-eight high school students representing all 50 states gathered in a replica U.S. Senate chamber in Boston earlier this month and passed the Students First Act, a comprehensive A.I. policy for K-12 schools, by a vote of 82 to 16.

The students were hosted by the Edward M. Kennedy Institute, AASA, The School Superintendents Association, and Day of AI, a nonprofit launched out of MIT's RAISE A.I. literacy initiative. AASA plans to distribute the bill's text to its 10,000 member school leaders, many of whom are currently drafting their own A.I. rules without federal guidance.

The bill's provisions include banning A.I. on all graded tests, requiring A.I. literacy instruction as soon as students receive classroom devices, and allowing A.I. for editing, brainstorming and studying after eighth grade but not for writing. It also requires that suspected misuse be reviewed by A.I. detection software and two school officials rather than detection software alone, and calls for federal funding to support A.I. literacy programs.

Jeffrey Riley, executive director of Day of AI and former Massachusetts education commissioner, said: "The adults themselves haven't been able to come to consensus on this. Let them lead the way."

<break time="1.0s"/>

From the research front, Texas Tech University researchers Erik P. Bucy and Milad Jalalian Ebrahimi have published a comparative analysis of A.I. adoption in three major newsrooms, with findings that carry implications beyond journalism. Their study, published in Digital Information World, examined Reuters, the BBC and The Guardian.

Reuters uses internally developed tools for financial data analysis and press release processing, and can publish some breaking financial alerts in six to eight seconds. A BBC study co-published with the European Broadcasting Union found that A.I. assistants misrepresented news content 45% of the time. The Guardian, after initially barring generative A.I. from producing publishable text, updated its policy in March 2026 to allow limited uses with senior editor approval.

The researchers introduce the concept of a "verification tax," the time spent correcting A.I. errors, as a factor that can offset efficiency gains. No A.I.-assisted content at the BBC is published without journalist review.

<break time="1.0s"/>

And in Investing in Innovation, Axios reports exclusively that Coursera is investing one hundred million dollars in LearnVector, a new A.I. education company founded by Andrew Ng, who also serves as Coursera's own chairman and co-founder. The investment gives Coursera roughly a one-third ownership stake in LearnVector.

LearnVector's stated goal is to build A.I. agents that function as personal tutors, adapting to individual learners until they demonstrate mastery of a concept. The first LearnVector products are targeted for early 2027, with a focus on education for working adults. The deal required a special board committee review because of Ng's dual role as Coursera chairman and LearnVector founder.

Coursera CEO Greg Hart told Axios the investment targets something more durable than standard chatbot interactions. The company has not released products to date.

<break time="1.0s"/>

That's this week's Innovation Pulse. Full coverage and source links at innovating higher ed dot com.

leadStory.headline: OpenAI Offers 100,000 Academic Researchers Free Access to GPT-5.6 Through 2027

The program targets researchers in biology, chemistry, computer science, engineering, mathematics and physics. The first 10,000 researchers will begin receiving access this summer at institutions including the Institute for Advanced Study. "Our strategy is not to decide which scientific problems deserve attention or try to solve them all ourselves," OpenAI said in a statement. "It is to put capable tools in the hands of the research community and let researchers pursue the questions they know best."

Researchers in A.I. fields have argued that meaningful independent evaluation requires access to model weights and training data. OpenAI says restricting access to model weights helps prevent misuse, but researchers counter that limited access hampers independent evaluations of model behavior, reproducibility and safety.

The program is aimed broadly at math and science fields rather than those studying A.I. itself, meaning the researchers most focused on understanding and auditing the technology are excluded from its benefits.

quickHits.headline: Former AI Critic Launches National Index to Rank Campus AI Readiness
quickHits.summary:
Two years ago, Scott Latham was one of academia's leading voices against artificial intelligence. In a June 2024 editorial for Inside Higher Ed, the University of Massachusetts Lowell business professor implored faculty to "pump the brakes on artificial intelligence in higher education," warning that robots would take their jobs.

Today, Latham not only uses A.I. in his own classroom — he has launched the AI Campus Index, an independent national ranking system that measures how well colleges and universities deploy A.I. for students, faculty and operations. The index, which launched last month and is not affiliated with any company or university, scores institutions across six areas: A.I. in the classroom, campus life, operations, governance, research and workforce readiness. The total possible score is 350 points, with classroom use weighted most heavily at 85 possible points.

Latham told Inside Higher Ed that two things shifted his perspective: A.I. capabilities evolved faster than he anticipated, and concerns about higher education's long-term viability deepened. He now describes A.I. as an opportunity rather than a threat. This past semester, his students used A.I. to write business proposals for the Boys and Girls Club of Greater Lowell.

Latham still believes A.I. will displace some faculty — specifically those who refuse to engage with the technology. "The faculty that it's going to put out of a job are those that continue to resist and don't experiment," he told Inside Higher Ed.

The index uses Claude and proprietary algorithms to score institutions, and Latham says he hopes it will serve as a consumer transparency tool for students, families and policymakers.

quickHits.headline: Miami Dade College Draws 2,000 Students to AI Courses in Two Years
quickHits.summary:
When Miami Dade College launched its associate degree in applied A.I. in fall 2023, enrollment immediately exceeded expectations. Instead of a typical new-program cohort of a few dozen students, more than 750 enrolled in A.I. courses in the first academic year. By fall 2025, more than 2,000 students of varying ages and backgrounds were taking A.I. courses at the college, according to a first-person account published in Issues in Science and Technology by Antonio Delgado Fornaguera, MDC's vice president of innovation and technology partnerships.

The demographics stand out. Over the first three academic years, roughly 60% of students were older than 26, and about 30% were older than 41 — experienced professionals and career changers seeking an on-ramp into applied A.I. roles. Women comprised approximately 40% of enrollment, double the typical rate in computer science programs.

The curriculum was built around employer input from a Business and Industry Leadership Team of A.I. professionals and hiring managers. "We don't need every hire to build new models from scratch," BILT member and AI Leadership Institute CEO Noelle Russell told MDC curriculum designers. "We need people who can work with data, test outputs, document decisions, and apply AI in a real process where mistakes have consequences."

To scale faculty capacity, MDC added seven new full-time faculty members and more than 20 part-time adjuncts, supported by funding from a local foundation. Industry partners including Amazon Web Services, Google, OpenAI and NVIDIA provided additional training and curriculum materials.

MDC has since co-founded the National Applied A.I. Consortium, which has trained more than 3,000 faculty and staff across 550 colleges and universities in 48 states.

quickHits.headline: Data Center Boom Drives 42% Pay Premium for Electricians and Trades Workers
quickHits.summary:
Installation and maintenance jobs at data centers pay 42% more than comparable positions in other fields, according to an Indeed analysis cited by The New York Times — a gap fueling intense competition for electricians, carpenters and other skilled trades workers as A.I. companies race to build infrastructure.

The scale of the buildout has no precedent, according to experts quoted in the Times report. Data centers could triple their power use in the United States over the next three years, reaching 12% of the country's total electricity consumption, according to a Department of Energy-backed study.

In markets with heavy data center activity — including Dallas and Northern Virginia — workers are switching employers for signing bonuses and higher per diem rates. The competition for labor is beginning to affect other sectors. Economist Mario Iacobacci told the Times: "The resources are very limited, so decisions to build one thing kind of drag from another."

The data center boom has offset flagging construction in other sectors, including office construction, which never recovered after the pandemic, and offshore wind, which has faced political opposition.

Google has announced funding for the training of tens of thousands of new U.S. electricians, including a $10 million grant for electrical worker nonprofits. BlackRock is investing $100 million in skilled trades training.

Longer-term, Jeff Strohl of Georgetown University's Center on Education and the Workforce told the Times that the ideal scenario — workers transitioning to a housing boom after data center construction peaks — is "probably not likely."

quickHits.headline: Compass Datacenters Launches Mississippi's First Data Center Workforce Training Program at Community College
quickHits.summary:
Compass Datacenters and Meridian Community College have launched Mississippi's first Mechanical, Electrical and Information Technology Data Center Pathway Program, creating a direct pipeline from the classroom to data center jobs in a state where competition for skilled trades workers is especially intense, The AI Journal reported.

The 14-week program requires no degree or prior experience. Compass is funding full-tuition scholarships for the inaugural cohort. Ten industry partners — including Schneider Electric, Siemens, Vertiv and Rosendin — are supporting the first class, which begins this fall following a two-day career fair on July 31 and August 1 at MCC's Riley Workforce Development Center.

The program is modeled on a Compass initiative launched in Red Oak, Texas, now in its second year. That program is waitlisted, and graduates have landed positions paying 30 to 50% above local median salaries with companies including CBRE, Schneider Electric and Siemens. The Texas program has since expanded to Texas State Technical College campuses in Waco and Abilene.

Meridian Community College serves more than 3,500 students annually and offers more than 40 career and technical education programs. Upon completion, the Compass campus in Meridian is projected to represent an estimated $10 billion investment including future tenant equipment.

"When we build in a community, we commit to it for the long haul," said Compass CEO Chris Crosby. "The people who live here should have every opportunity to benefit from the growth happening in their backyard."

The data center industry faces a shortfall of more than 500,000 skilled trade professionals annually, according to Compass.

quickHits.headline: 98 High School Students From All 50 States Draft National AI Policy for Schools
quickHits.summary:
Ninety-eight high school students representing all 50 states gathered in a replica U.S. Senate chamber in Boston earlier this month and passed the Students First Act — a comprehensive A.I. policy for K-12 schools — by a vote of 82 to 16, NPR reported.

The students were hosted by the Edward M. Kennedy Institute for the United States Senate, AASA (The School Superintendents Association) and Day of AI, a nonprofit launched out of MIT's RAISE A.I. literacy initiative. AASA plans to distribute the bill's text to its 10,000 member school leaders, many of whom are currently drafting their own A.I. rules without federal guidance.

The bill's provisions include: banning A.I. on all graded tests; requiring A.I. literacy instruction as soon as students receive classroom devices, covering misinformation, plagiarism, bias, student privacy, appropriate academic use and A.I.'s environmental impact; allowing A.I. for editing, brainstorming and studying after eighth grade but not for writing; requiring that suspected misuse be reviewed by A.I. detection software and two school officials rather than software alone; and requiring teachers to personally investigate before reporting suspected A.I. misuse to administrators.

The bill also addresses teacher use, permitting A.I. for lesson planning, practice materials and feedback, while requiring each teacher to post a clear written A.I. usage policy each semester.

Students debated school funding inequities when discussing the A.I. literacy requirement, ultimately adding a provision calling for federal funding support. They also agreed that school chatbots detecting a student in emotional distress should alert school officials rather than fulfill the student's request.

"The adults themselves haven't been able to come to consensus on this," said Jeffrey Riley, executive director of Day of AI and former Massachusetts education commissioner. "Let them lead the way."

quickHits.headline: AI Newsroom Study Finds Diverging Strategies and a 'Verification Tax' on Speed
quickHits.summary:
A.I. adoption in newsrooms reflects each outlet's funding model and editorial values rather than a single industry-wide approach, according to a comparative analysis by Texas Tech University researchers Erik P. Bucy and Milad Jalalian Ebrahimi published in Digital Information World.

The researchers analyzed public documents through 2025, including official A.I. policy statements, editorial guidelines, trial reports and industry presentations, from three major outlets: Reuters, the BBC and The Guardian. Their findings illustrate the range of choices facing any organization, including universities, that is integrating A.I. into content production.

Reuters, which uses internally developed tools for real-time financial data analysis and corporate press release processing, can publish some breaking financial alerts in six to eight seconds. A BBC study co-published with the European Broadcasting Union found that A.I. assistants misrepresented news content 45% of the time. The Guardian, after barring generative A.I. from producing publishable text, updated its policy in March 2026 to allow limited uses with senior editor approval.

The researchers introduce the concept of a "verification tax" — the time journalists spend correcting A.I. errors — as a factor that can offset the technology's efficiency gains.

Reuters uses Lynx Insight for financial data analysis and Fact Genie for press releases. The BBC's tools, At a Glance and BBC Style Assist, summarize and reformat stories; no A.I.-assisted content is published without journalist review.

quickHits.headline: Coursera Invests $100 Million in Andrew Ng's New AI Tutoring Startup
quickHits.summary:
Coursera is investing $100 million in LearnVector, a new A.I. education company founded by Andrew Ng — Coursera's own chairman and co-founder — Axios reported exclusively. The investment gives Coursera roughly a third ownership stake in LearnVector, and the two companies will explore commercial partnerships combining LearnVector's A.I. technology with Coursera's content library and global distribution network.

LearnVector's stated goal is to build A.I. agents that function as personal tutors, adapting to individual learners and practicing with them until they demonstrate mastery of a concept. The first LearnVector products are targeted for early 2027. The startup is focused on education for working adults, not K-12 or university students.

Coursera CEO Greg Hart told Axios the investment is aimed at building something more durable than chatbot interactions. "If it's not tied to a much more holistic, pedagogically rigorous view of the skill that you are trying to develop, I think that's going to be a shorter, less fulfilling, and less engaging outcome," Hart said.

The deal required a special board committee review because of Ng's dual role as Coursera chairman and LearnVector founder. Hart said Coursera is also making its own A.I. investments but views LearnVector as likely to generate complementary ideas. "We had an opportunity to invest at the formation of a brand new company from one of the world's foremost experts on AI," Hart said.

Axios described the investment as one of the largest public bets by an established education technology company on A.I.-native learning.
